results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Bringer of the Last Gift, Superior Spider-Man and Town Greeter.
results.text:
I'll start by checking the three requested cards and what real decks run them with.

The three cards point to a self-mill plan: Town Greeter fills the graveyard, and Spider-Man and Bringer both want creatures there. Nothing in results plays all three together, so I'll look at the Golgari Roots shell Town Greeter sits in and the current field.

Two shells look relevant: Golgari Roots (the mill deck Town Greeter lives in) and Dimir Midrange (the most-played blue-black removal and creature package). I'll pull both reference lists and check the candidate cards.

Several staples in the Dimir and Golgari lists are not legal here (Go for the Throat, Cut Down, Sheoldred's Edict), so I'll check the replacements. Next I need to find ways to put Bringer into the graveyard on purpose, plus lands and graveyard-recursion cards.

Good: Honest Rutstein, Xu-Ifit, Vampire Soulcaller, Graveshifter and Live or Die are all creature-recursion options. Next I'll check the mana base and the remaining creature and mill candidates.

The mill pieces check out. Llanowar Wastes, Tyvar and Haywire Mite are not legal, so I'll avoid them. Next I'll check sideboard candidates against the field and run the first deck check.

The first check passed with no errors. It flagged 14 green sources and a recommended 24 lands, so I'll go to 23 lands with a fifth Forest and cut Osteomancer Adept. I'll recheck that version and test the Spider-Man mana.

Both checks are clean: no errors or warnings, 23 lands, 7 blue sources. The Spider-Man-plus-blue-source draw is 39% by turn 6, so the line is slow but real. Submitting the deck now.

The checker flagged three recursion cards as rarely played. Each one does a specific job for Bringer, so I'll keep them and resubmit with those reasons.

I built a Golgari mill-and-reanimate brew around Bringer, Spider-Man and Town Greeter, with a light blue splash for Spider-Man. The chosen direction was Golgari because it gives the cleanest mana. A Dimir base would have needed a green splash just for a 1/1 Town Greeter, and Dimir's double-blue cards clash with that. The plan is to mill creatures into the graveyard, then use Bitter Triumph to discard Bringer and cast Spider-Man as a copy of it for 4 mana. That should wipe the opponent's board, return creatures from both graveyards, and leave a 6/6 flyer. Its ETB firing on a cast copy is my reading of the rules, not a checked ruling. The line is slow: Spider-Man and a blue source are both in hand by turn 6 about 39% of the time, and the full line completes by turn 6 in only about 6.5% of games.

The deck is 37 spells and 23 lands, borrowing Golgari Roots' mana and mill cards and Dimir Midrange's black removal. Golgari Roots itself is only 0.3% of the field, so this is a brew, not a proven list. Legal stock cards I left out include Go for the Throat, Cut Down and Sheoldred's Edict. The sideboard is built against Izzet Aggro and Vivi Cauldron.

The copied trigger makes each player sacrifice all other creatures, then returns creature cards from both graveyards to the battlefield; Spider-Man stays as a 6/6 flyer

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Mightform Harmonizer, Spell Snare and Full Bore.
results.text:
I'll start by checking the three requested cards and what real decks run them with.

The three requested cards have no published list together, so I need to see what each one pairs with separately. Checking the landfall and warp packages and the Landfall reference list.

Three directions look possible:

1. **G/R landfall-warp:** Harmonizer's green landfall shell, with red warp creatures and burn. Full Bore's haste and trample fit warp here.
2. **G/U landfall:** the same green core with blue, where Spell Snare fits, and Full Bore is splashed.
3. **Boros or Izzet aggro with Full Bore:** this drops Harmonizer and Spell Snare, so it misses the request.

Next I'll pull the card text for the candidates in the green and red packages.

Screaming Nemesis shows as banned in Standard, so it stays out of the deck. Next I'll check the red removal and the remaining red and green creatures.

Red gives this shell its burn, its warp creatures and Full Bore's haste, so I'm building G/R landfall-warp with a blue splash for Spell Snare. Before I finalize the mana, I'll check the fixing lands.

Fabled Passage and Evolving Wilds are both legal and fetch basics, so each counts as a land drop. Now I'll run the draft through check_deck, comparing its mana to the Landfall list I borrowed from.

The checker flags 17 lands, a low curve, and only 4 blue sources. The Landfall list it compared against runs about 25 lands, and this deck wants land drops for its engine. I'll move to 18 lands by cutting Bushwhack, and add a third Island so Spell Snare has more blue sources.

The remaining warning is the generic ramp heuristic. This deck has 18 lands plus four Llanowar Elves, so it has 22 mana sources. Before submitting, I'll check the odds of getting blue for Spell Snare and green for the Harmonizer line.

Blue is available on turn 4 about 61% of the time, which is workable for a two-copy splash. The last check is that the basic lands were looked up, so I'll confirm them before submitting.

The checker wants a reason for five blue sources, since builds around a card usually run six or more. Spell Snare is a two-copy splash, so I'll state that instead of adding blue sources.

The only card note is on Tannuk, which real players rarely choose. I'll keep it and answer the note, since its landfall draw is what this deck is built around.

I built a green-red landfall deck around Mightform Harmonizer, with Full Bore and two Spell Snares. It's a brew: no published list plays these three together. The accepted list is 18 lands, with seven Forests, six Mountains, three Islands, Evolving Wilds and Fabled Passage.

Three directions were on the table: green-red landfall-warp, green-blue landfall with Full Bore splashed, or a red aggro shell that drops Harmonizer and Spell Snare. I chose green-red because red supplies the burn, the warp creatures, and the haste and trample Full Bore gives warped creatures. The green core (Llanowar Elves, Bristly Bill, Tifa, Mossborn Hydra) is borrowed from the Landfall list. Spell Snare is a two-copy blue splash, so it's the weakest card in the deck.

The main line is Harmonizer hard-cast on turn 4, then a land drop on turn 5 doubles its power from 4 to 8, and Full Bore adds 3 more for an 11-damage attack. The tool estimates that line is fully drawn by turn 5 in only about 1.9% of games, so expect it to be a plan you build toward rather than a reliable turn-5 kill.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Airbender Ascension, Bramble Familiar and Appa, Steadfast Guardian.
results.text:
I'll start by checking the three requested cards and what real decks run them with.

Appa is the most-played of the three, in Rogue lists. I'll pull the Rogue and Selesnya shells to compare.

Rogue is the big shell (325 lists) and runs Appa, but it's a three-to-five color mess. Selesnya Offense is green-heavy and has almost no white. Before picking a direction, I'll search for airbend and white/green payoffs in the card pool.

The airbend package is mostly white: Appa, Aang the Last Airbender, Airbending Lesson, Airbender's Reversal, Glider Staff, and Avatar's Wrath. I'll check white removal and cheap white and blue creatures that work with it.

White has enough airbend payoffs and cheap creatures, and Bramble Familiar is green, so a G/W build keeps all three requested cards. I'll look at the green creatures, the G/W lands, and the Selesnya package.

I have enough to pick a direction. Next I'll confirm legality and the recent field numbers for the remaining candidate cards.

Get Lost is heavily played in Standard. The airbend cards and most white creatures have little or no tournament data, so the deck will be a brew. I'll check the first draft of the list.

The draft passes check_deck with no errors or warnings. The mana is in range for the curve (average mana value 2.38), and Appa comes online by turn 3 on the play about 39% of the time. Last, I'll validate the sideboard candidates against the field's Artifacts, Dimir, Izzet and Reanimator threats.

Sideboard candidates are all legal and the Reanimator and Artifacts threats show up in the field data. I'll check the full 60 plus 15 sideboard before submitting.

Check passes with 60 main and 15 sideboard, no errors or warnings. Submitting as a brew.

I built a G/W airbend midrange deck with all three cards. It's a brew, submitted at 60 main plus 15 sideboard, and it passed the checker with no errors or warnings.

Three directions I considered:
- **G/W airbend (chosen):** keeps all three requested cards. Bramble Familiar and Llanowar Elves ramp into Appa on turn 3, and the cheap creatures feed Airbender Ascension's quest counters.
- **W/U airbend:** strong airbend creatures, but it drops Bramble Familiar, which you asked for.
- **Rogue-style multicolor with Appa:** Rogue is the most-played shell that runs Appa, but it's a four- or five-color mana base and has no Ascension.

The plan is to land Llanowar Elves and Bramble Familiar early, flash in Appa on turn 3 to airbend both mana dorks, and recast them for {2} each. Airbender Ascension then builds quest counters, and at four its end-step trigger blinks Appa to airbend again while the flyers attack.

Honest caveats:
- Appa is in 3 copies. I wrote in the submission that legendary cards cap copies, which is not accurate. Three was a judgment call to limit legend-rule clunk, and four would be legal.
- Appa comes down by turn 3 on the play about 39% of the time.
- The win line on turn 6 has every card drawn in only about 7.6% of games. That is a fragile line, not a reliable one.
- Most of the airbend and white payoffs have no recent tournament data, so the list is untested.

Turn 2 second mana dork; turn 3 has enough mana to flash in Appa.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Abandon Attachments, Firebending Lesson and Combustion Technique.
results.text:
The deck is submitted as a mono-red Lesson brew, 60 cards with 17 lands. I checked three directions: mono-red Lessons, Boros Lessons (white Lessons plus Boros aggro), and Izzet Lessons (blue Lessons plus Izzet Aggro). I picked mono-red because all three requested cards are red, Abandon Attachments is hybrid, and Izzet Aggro's red core is the most-played shell (12% of the field). Blue Lessons barely appear in recent results.

**The plan:** Pressure early with Hired Claw, Emberheart Challenger and Burnout Bashtronaut, and clear blockers with Burst Lightning, Firebending Lesson and Lightning Strike. Abandon Attachments fills the graveyard with Lessons, which scales Combustion Technique into a hard removal spell. Nova Hellkite, Ran and Shaw and Bonehoard Dracosaur close games. Turn 5 is the target win turn.

**Things you should know:**
- **Screaming Nemesis is banned in Standard.** The Izzet and Boros menu entries list it, but `card_info` shows it as banned, so I left it out.
- **The only published list with these three cards is a mono-red Lesson list** that placed 13th. I borrowed the Izzet Aggro red core and kept the Lesson payoffs. Jeong Jeong and Ran and Shaw have no tournament results yet, so treat them as untested.
- **The checker flagged 17 lands** against a heuristic of about 23. I kept 17 because the deck has five 5-drops, Lesson kickers, and mana sinks like Burnout Bashtronaut's pump. Real Izzet lists run about 24 with manlands, which this build doesn't have.
- **Bonehoard Dracosaur drew a card note** (0% of recent decks). I kept it: it's the red card-advantage engine and a Dragon for Ran and Shaw's graveyard check.
- **Draw odds (no mulligan, on the play):** 96% to have a land by turn 3, and 93% to have at least one burn spell or Lesson by turn 3.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Ashling, Rekindled, Sunderflock and Bounce Off.
results.text:
I'll start by checking the three requested cards and what real decks run them with.

The three cards don't appear together in any list. Sunderflock and Ashling show up in Rogue, so I'll pull that archetype, the meta, and the Elemental pool.

Sunderflock's discount depends on Elementals, and the pool has many of them. I'll check the Simic Ouroboroid shell (it runs Bounce Off), a few high-MV Elementals, and the Sunderflock-adjacent cards.

Sunderflock's discount only works with big Elementals, and Ashling's mana ability can pay for it. Next I'll survey the blue-red cards that could fill out that shell.

I have enough candidates to sketch the shell. Before I commit I need exact text and legality for the cards I'm considering from outside the requested three.

Stormchaser's Talent is banned in Standard, so the Rogue and Lessons lists that run it are outdated. I'll leave it out. Now I'll check the draft against Rogue's mana, since that's the shell whose mana I'm borrowing.

The check passes with no errors or warnings, but it recommends about 24 lands and I'm at 23. I'll move one more land in and cut Into the Flood Maw, the weakest of the cheap bounce spells, since Bounce Off already fills that role.

The deck is now at 24 lands with no warnings. Before submitting, I'll check the main risk: whether a big Elemental to discount Sunderflock shows up in time.

The odds are honest but not fast: a discount Elemental and Ashling are both in hand by turn 5 about 36% of the time. Submitting now.

The checker flagged Summon: Shiva as rarely played. I'm keeping it because it's an Elemental, and the deck needs 4-7 mana Elementals for Sunderflock's discount. Quantum Riddler isn't an Elemental, so Sunderflock would bounce it. Resubmitting with that reason.

I built a blue-red Elemental deck around Ashling, Sunderflock and Bounce Off, and it's accepted as a brew. Ashling flips to Rimebound to add 2 mana for each 4+ mana-value spell, which pays for a 6-drop Elemental like Ice Flan. Ice Flan's mana value then cuts Sunderflock to about {1}{U}{U}, and its ETB bounces the opponent's non-Elementals while your Elementals stay on the battlefield. Bounce Off and red burn handle early threats until then.

I chose this direction over two others. A Simic Ouroboroid build with Bounce Off would have Sunderflock bounce its own non-Elemental creatures, so Sunderflock fits poorly there. A Dimir build had too few cheap Elementals to power the discount. The Rogue list was useful only for its blue-red mana.

The line is slow. Odds are honest: Ashling is in hand by turn 5 about 57% of the time, and a discount Elemental by turn 5 about 65%, with both by turn 5 only about 36%. The win line's cards are all drawn by turn 5 in just 6.4% of simulated games. Stormchaser's Talent is banned in Standard, so the Rogue and Lessons lists that run it are outdated. The checker flagged Summon: Shiva as rarely played, and I kept it because it is one of the few 4-6 mana Elementals that doesn't clash with Sunderflock.

Turn 4 (4 lands + Ashling's 2 mana) 6-drop Elemental; its ETB taps and stuns the opponent's best creature, and its MV 6 makes Sunderflock cost about {1}{U}{U}.
Turn 5: cast for about 3 mana with Ice Flan out (Ashling's mana helps); ETB bounces all opposing non-Elementals while the Elementals stay, leaving a 5/5 flier to win.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Insatiable Avarice, Doomsday Excruciator and Archenemy's Charm.
results.text:
The deck is submitted as a mono-black brew (24 black sources) with the Mono-Black shell as its donor. Its plan is to control the early game with the Charm, Triumph and Heartless Act, then cast Doomsday Excruciator (BBBBBB) on six Swamps. Insatiable Avarice's draw-three mode, cast on the opponent after the Excruciator resolves, leaves them with 3 cards in library against your 6, and your extra upkeep draws should make them deck first around turn 10. The Excruciator is a 6/6 flyer, so it also pressures them before that.

I weighed three directions. Mono-black was the only one where Archenemy's Charm (BBB) and Excruciator (six black pips) are reliably castable on curve, and the Mono-Black results and the menu's black cards support it. Dimir plays the Excruciator, but blue makes six black pips unreliable. Golgari splits its mana too thinly for the same reason.

Caveats: the Excruciator decking line is slow and needs six black sources, which I estimate at about 50% by turn 8 on the play; draw_odds can't count six copies, so that figure is a hypergeometric estimate. The full line (Excruciator, Avarice, Excruciator again) is drawn by turn 10 in only about 43% of games, so the Excruciator's attack is the practical win condition.

winLine.does: Cast on 6 black sources: each player exiles all but the bottom six cards of their library; a 6/6 flyer that draws you an extra card each upkeep.
Draw-three mode (BB) targeting the opponent: they draw 3 and lose 3 life, leaving them 3 cards in library while you keep 6.
Your extra upkeep draws run you 2 per turn against their 1, so the opponent draws from an empty library first around turn 10; the 6/6 flyer also attacks in the meantime.

Treat it as a midrange-value deck with a strong early curve, not a reliable turn-5 kill. The deck is 23 lands and 37 spells, and it passed check_deck with no errors or warnings.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Resonating Lute, Inevitable Defeat and Jeskai Revelation.
results.text:
I built a Jeskai Control deck with a black splash for Inevitable Defeat, and the submission was accepted with no warnings. The plan is to control the board with cheap instants and Day of Judgment, draw cards with Stock Up and Consult the Star Charts, then finish with Jeskai Revelation and Quantum Riddler. Resonating Lute doubles every land's mana for instants and sorceries, which pays for Revelation and makes black available from any land for Inevitable Defeat.

I considered three directions. A Mardu Rogue build would have run Inevitable Defeat as its core but had no clean place for Lute or Revelation. An Izzet tempo build would have used Lute and Revelation but dropped the requested Defeat. I chose the Jeskai Control shell because it is the only one that naturally runs Lute and Revelation, and it borrows its removal and card-draw package.

Weak points to know about:
- The mana is stretched. It runs 13 white sources against about 17 in the Jeskai Control lists, and 6 black sources, which gives about 75% to have a black source by turn 6 before Lute.
- The full win line is rarely assembled early: the model puts the whole line drawn by turn 7 at about 2%. The deck depends on Stock Up and Consult to find its threats.
- Marang River Regent, Quantum Riddler and Revelation are the only real threats, so the deck is light on board presence.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Dáin's Company, Dwarven Mauler and Kíli the Resourceful.
results.text:

The plan is to start with Dáin's Company or Kíli, use Dwarven Mattock and Dáin Ironfoot's Axe to load up a Dwarf, then remove blockers with Thorin, Mountain-king and Mjölnir. The Mjölnir line doubles the damage of an equipped legendary Dwarf, which is the lethal turn-5 line. Honest odds: the full line is in hand by turn 5 in only about 2% of games, so this is a card-quality and consistency bet, not a reliable curve-out.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Greedy Freebooter, The Sackville-Bagginses and Umbral Collar Zealot.
results.text:
I built a mono-black sacrifice deck around the three requested cards and submitted it. It's a brew: no published list runs Greedy Freebooter, The Sackville-Bagginses and Umbral Collar Zealot together, so there was no proven list to copy.

**Plan:** Turn 1 Freebooter, turn 2 Zealot, turn 3 Sackville sacrificing a dying Freebooter to draw and make a Treasure. Bloodghast recurs off land drops as endless fodder, Sephiroth and Liliana, Dreadhorde General turn the sacrifices into cards, and about 10 cheap black removal spells handle early threats. The sacrifice engine fits in one colour, so the deck runs 22 Swamps with no splash.

**Direction chosen:** I considered three. A Golgari build (Zealot's closest real home, Golgari Roots) would need green ramp and a splash; a Dimir build would add blue bounce without sacrifice payoff. Mono-black won because it makes the one-drop Freebooter and the BB Bloodghast reliable, and it borrows only the Overlord and Bloodghast package from the menu.

**Honest odds:** Being on the play, a Freebooter appears by turn 3 about 49% of the time, and all of Freebooter, Zealot and Sackville together only 8%. This is a fragile, unproven deck: the sacrifice payoffs are strong once fodder lands, but it has no tested results behind it. The sideboard is built against the field (Murder, Withering Torment, Massacre Wurm for the go-wide decks, Duress for the control decks).

results.prompt: Brew me a Pioneer deck built around Sentinel of the Nameless City, Abrupt Decay and Tear Asunder.

I considered three directions: a Golgari sacrifice shell borrowed from Jund Sacrifice, a mono-green Devotion build with a black splash, and a Golgari midrange deck with more threats. I chose the first, and borrowed only Ygra, Deadly Dispute, Fatal Push and the Golgari dual lands from Jund Sacrifice. I dropped its red cards and most of its Food engine, because that engine needs too many enablers to be reliable without red.

The plan is to ramp with Elvish Mystic and Llanowar Elves, land Sentinel on turn 3, and hold Abrupt Decay and Tear Asunder for the threats that matter. The deck runs 21 lands plus six mana creatures, and it wins with Cavalier of Thorns, Ygra and Overlord of the Hauntwoods once the blockers are gone. Honest odds: the stated win line (every card drawn by turn 5) happens in only about 2.1% of games, so this is a grindy deck that wins by controlling the board and then pressing, not one that wins on curve.

results.prompt: Brew me a Modern deck built around Fight Rigging, Turntimber Symbiosis and Slumbering Trudge.
results.text:

The three cards don't appear together in any published list, so I'll look at the pieces they need: hideaway payoffs, stun and big-creature enablers, and green ramp.

The engine is clear: Fight Rigging adds a +1/+1 counter each combat, and a creature with power 7 or more lets you cast the hideaway card free. Trudge (6/6 for X=0) and Turntimber Symbiosis both put big bodies in play. Next I'll check the candidate enablers and the green shells on the menu.

Mono-green looks like the cleanest host: Trudge, Fight Rigging and Turntimber all want green mana. Before choosing threats, I'll check green removal and early creatures, plus a few top-end cards.

I'm choosing the mono-green direction. Three directions I weighed:

1. **Mono-green Trudge + Fight Rigging ramp** (chosen): every green source supports Trudge's cheap 6/6 body and Rigging's counters, and Turntimber and Boseiju are both green.
2. **Green-blue with Neoform's package** (Ghalta, Summoner's Pact, Nourishing Shoal): more card quality, but blue dilutes the green needed for Trudge, Rigging and the 6-drops.
3. **Gruul with burn** (Lightning Bolt, Ragavan-style aggression): the Trudge/Rigging engine is slow and doesn't need aggressive redirection.

Next I'll check the draft and the odds of the key turn-3 play.

The check passes with no errors, but the land count is light for a deck with seven 6-drops and three 7-drops. I'll swap one Elvish Mystic for a Forest, then recheck and look at the odds a turn later.

The deck checks clean, with the Amulet Titan land warning explained by its fetch lands. Submitting it as a brew.

I built a mono-green brew around Fight Rigging and Slumbering Trudge, with Turntimber Symbiosis as a late-game creature tutor and extra land. The deck was accepted with no warnings.

**Plan:** Turn 1 Slumbering Trudge with X=0 gives a 6/6 that enters stunned, so it can't attack for a few turns but still works as a target. Turn 3 Fight Rigging puts a +1/+1 counter on Trudge at combat, making it 7/7, which lets you cast the hideaway card free. From there, the deck ramps into 6–7 drops like Vorinclex, Primeval Titan and Craterhoof.

**Direction:** I chose mono-green over green-blue (Neoform-style Ghalta and Nourishing Shoal) and Gruul burn. Trudge, Rigging and Turntimber all need steady green mana, and the green ramp package (Green Sun's Zenith, Primeval Titan, Boseiju) came from Amulet Titan.

**Odds and caveats:** On the play, Trudge and Fight Rigging are both in hand by turn 4 about 21% of the time, and by turn 6 about 29%. No published list runs these three cards together, so the line is untested. The deck is also light on interaction, with only seven removal spells, and the land count (21 lands including Turntimber) is below the typical ~21.2 recommendation for this curve.

results.text:

The third is Izzet tempo with Call Forth as a finisher. I chose the first because Apex and Call Forth only cascade when cast, so cheating them into play loses most of their value, and the Izzet route can't reliably reach 8 mana.

The plan is to ramp with Lotus Petal, Mox Diamond, Llanowar Elves and Exploration, use Bloodbraid Elf and Violent Outburst to chain free spells, and cast Call Forth at 8 mana or Apex at 10 for four cascades. Natural Order is a backup way to put Apex in for 4 mana.

Apex and Call Forth each show up by turn 7 about 39% of the time. The full win line is drawn by turn 7 in only 1.4% of games, so this deck relies on its ramp and cascade density rather than a reliable combo.

Entomb is listed as banned in this Legacy pool, though your Esper Tempo list runs four, so I left it out.

results.prompt: Brew me a Legacy deck built around Arclight Phoenix, Buried Alive and Flow State.
results.text:
I built a blue-red Phoenix spells deck with a light black splash, borrowing the Izzet Tempo mana and cantrip shell. The deck is a brew, not a copy of a published list. I weighed three directions: Izzet spells (chosen), a Dimir base with a red splash, and a black Reanimator build. Izzet won because Phoenix, Flow State, Dragon's Rage Channeler, Lightning Bolt and Murktide all reward the same instant-and-sorcery density, and Izzet Tempo is 8% of the field. Dimir would have needed a red splash for Phoenix and Bolt, and Reanimator drops Phoenix and Flow State entirely.

**The plan:** Buried Alive (two copies) puts Arclight Phoenix into the graveyard, and a turn that casts three instants or sorceries returns it at beginning of combat with haste and flying. Flow State, Brainstorm, Ponder, Lightning Bolt, Force of Will, Daze and Murktide Regent supply the spell count and graveyard fuel. Black comes only from five sources, enough for Buried Alive and two Fatal Push.

**The honest odds:** The full line (Buried Alive, then two cheap spells, on turn 5) completes in about 3% of games. Buried Alive is in hand or drawn by turn 5 on the play about 34% of the time, and Phoenix about 46%. Phoenix also works as a plain 4-mana flier, so the deck is not dead without the line, but it is a slower, less consistent plan than the stock Izzet list.

The deck passed `check_deck` with 18 lands and a 15-card sideboard aimed at Dimir and Tron (Force of Negation, Consign to Memory, Pyroblast, Meltdown).

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Aurora Eidolon, Sandstorm Eidolon and Spirit Mascot.
results.text:
I built a Boros (R/W) aggro deck around the three cards, with the white core of the Mono-White Aggro list. It's a brew, and the engine is thin: the deck has only nine multicolored spells to return the Eidolons, so expect that payoff in maybe half of games.

**Direction chosen:** Boros aggro. Spirit Mascot is itself R/W, so it fits the colors, and the tournament shell gave me proven white creatures and burn. The other two directions were a mono-white deck splashing red only for Mascot, and playing the Eidolons in another color pair, which needs multicolored spells I couldn't find in quantity. I went with Boros because it keeps all three requested cards in their intended colors.

**The plan:** Turn 2 Spirit Mascot, turn 3 Skyknight Legionnaire, turn 4 Battle Screech, then flash in flyers and burn. Mascot grows whenever cards leave the graveyard: Battle Screech and Prismatic Strands flashback, Lunarch Veteran's disturb, and an Eidolon returning to hand. Sandstorm Eidolon's R ability makes a blocker unable to block for the final attack.

**Things to know:**
- Lightning Helix, Boros Charm and Figure of Destiny are not legal in Pauper, so they couldn't go in.
- The Eidolons are 2/2s for four. They are value cards, not threats, and they only work with a multicolored spell to bring them back.
- The mana is 19 lands (4 Boros Garrison, 10 Plains, 5 Mountain): 14 white sources and 9 red. That's a bit under the tournament Boros lists on red.
- The sideboard is built against the field: Journey to Nowhere and Destroy Evil for Terror's big blue creatures, Red Elemental Blast for Terror and Faeries, Dust to Dust for Affinity and Synthesizer artifacts, and Holy Light and Electrickery for the X/1 creatures in Madness and Elves.

results.prompt: Brew me a Premodern deck built around Living Death.
results.text:
The deck is accepted as a brew: a black-based Living Death deck that uses the Reanimator/BG Survival pieces. I chose it over two other directions: a straight BG Survival list (more green creatures, but its 8-drop green fatties are slow) and a Moneyball Black list (no reason to be playing Living Death in it). The plan is to fill the graveyard with fatties by turn 3 using Buried Alive, Survival of the Fittest, Hidden Horror or a tutor, then cast Living Death on turn 5 to bring them back, with Phyrexian Gargantua drawing two on each return.

Living Death runs 3 copies, and six tutors (Diabolic Intent and Diabolic Tutor) plus Dark Ritual and Birds of Paradise help find and cast it. Honest odds from the draw tool: with three copies in 60 cards, you have about a 46% chance of seeing Living Death by turn 5 on the play, and about 53% by turn 6 on the draw. Buried Alive has the same 46% by turn 5. Reanimate and Animate Dead-style returns are the fallback when Living Death is missing, so the deck is still playable without it.

winLine.does: Turn 3: search for up to three fatties (Phyrexian Gargantua x2, Visara the Dreadful) and put them straight into the graveyard.
Turn 5: exiles all creatures from my graveyard, sacrifices my board and the opponent's board, then returns the exiled fatties to the battlefield; each Gargantua ETB draws two.
Next turn: tap to destroy whatever creature the opponent rebuilt with.
